title: Milan (Confessions 5–6)
hook: Augustine goes to hear Ambrose's style and stays for the substance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pears: a theft with no reason but the forbidden and the friends. Your line was why did I do it. What small thing did you catch yourself at? Day seven hundred thirty-five.

A job offer. The city of Milan needs a teacher of public speaking, and Augustine gets the post. He's a professional now: he teaches young men how to persuade a room. He arrives in Milan and, as part of settling in, goes to meet the bishop. It's Ambrose, the governor the crowd made bishop, the one who wrote to the emperor. Augustine has heard Ambrose is a superb speaker. So when Ambrose preaches, he goes to church. Not to pray. To review the performance.
screen: `A NEW JOB IN MILAN.` → `A PROFESSIONAL PERSUADER.` → `HE GOES TO REVIEW THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: Augustine tells it in Books Five and Six of the Confessions. First, the welcome. He says Ambrose received him like a father, and Augustine began to love him, not yet as a teacher of truth, he admits, just as a man who was kind to him. Then the sermons. Augustine sits there like a critic. Is the bishop as good as his reputation? He listens closely to the words and doesn't care about the content. He even enjoys the sweetness of the speaking. And then something happens he didn't plan. While he was opening his ears to how well Ambrose spoke, he says, how truly he spoke came in along with it, little by little. He couldn't separate the two. He came for the style, and the substance got in. One thing that got in was a way of reading the Old Testament. Augustine had found some of its stories crude. Ambrose kept repeating a line from Saint Paul. In the Douay-Rheims: "the letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth." Read for the spirit, and the hard passages opened up. And one more picture from Milan: Ambrose reading. His eyes moved over the page, his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were still. Augustine and his friends would come in, find him reading silently, sit a while without disturbing him, and leave. He wanted to talk to the bishop and couldn't get the time. He got the sermons instead.
screen: `RECEIVED LIKE A SON.` · `LISTENING AS A CRITIC.` · `THE TRUTH CAME IN WITH THE WORDS.` · `THE LETTER KILLETH.` · then, large: `CAME FOR THE STYLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone for their substance. Settle, and breathe. Think of a voice you hear often: a preacher, a coworker, a relative, someone online. Maybe their style dazzles you, or maybe it grates on you. Set the style aside for a minute. What are they actually saying? Is any of it true? Take one thing they said lately and say it back to yourself in plain, flat words, stripped of the delivery. The bell holds the time.
Milan. The city where Augustine went to judge Ambrose's speaking, and where the substance of it got through to him. Today's word.

Your line: came for the style. This week ran from Cyril's lectures and Martin's cloak, through Ambrose, Monica's tears and the pears, to Milan. Today, listen to one person past how they say it, to what they say. Day seven hundred thirty-five.
screen: `THIS WEEK: CYRIL · MARTIN · AMBROSE · MONICA · THE PEARS · MILAN.`

original.note: Latin: the sweetness of his speech — what Augustine says he enjoyed in Ambrose's sermons.

what it means: he went as a critic of the bishop's speaking, and the truth got in through the style.
what a scholar hears: Confessions 5.13–14 and 6.3–4: the sweetness of speech, the letter that kills, and Ambrose reading with his voice at rest.

notes: 2 Corinthians 3:6 Douay-Rheims (Challoner): confirm wording 'the letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth'.

Confessions 5.13.23–14.24 paraphrased: the post of rhetoric teacher at Milan (Symmachus not named); Ambrose receiving him 'like a father'; listening to test the eloquence; delight in the sweetness of speech; how truly he spoke entering with how eloquently, by degrees. Confirm. Original game uses the Latin 'suavitate sermonis' (5.13.23, 'delectabar suavitate sermonis'); confirm.

6.3.3–4 paraphrased: Ambrose reading silently, eyes on the page, voice and tongue at rest; visitors sitting a while and leaving; no time for conversation. 6.4.6: Ambrose often commending 2 Cor 3:6 as a rule for reading the Old Testament. Confirm.
'Saint Paul' named as author of 2 Corinthians, which is undisputed; confirm.
